title: Absolute chart Jacobians form a smooth positive cocycle
statement: Let $N$ be a smooth real $m$-manifold without boundary [def-sfb-smooth-real-manifold], with $m\geq0$. For smooth charts $x_i:U_i\to V_i\subseteq\mathbf R^m$ and $p\in U_i\cap U_j$, define $g_{ij}(p)=|\det D(x_j\circ x_i^{-1})(x_i(p))|$, where $D$ is the ordinary real derivative on the open coordinate domain and the determinant [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant] in dimension zero is $1$. Then $g_{ij}$ is smooth and strictly positive on $U_i\cap U_j$, and its reciprocal is smooth there. On $U_i$ one has $g_{ii}=1$; on $U_i\cap U_j$ one has $g_{ji}g_{ij}=1$; on $U_i\cap U_j\cap U_k$ one has $g_{ik}=g_{jk}g_{ij}$. These assertions hold for every choice of smooth charts compatible with the given atlas, with no orientation, separation, countability, or compactness hypothesis.

proof.text: If $m=0$, every derivative is the unique linear endomorphism of $\mathbf R^0$ and its determinant is the empty determinant $1$. Thus every $g_{ij}$ and its reciprocal is the constant $1$, which is smooth; all three identities are $1=1$. Empty overlaps impose no conditions. Henceforth assume $m\geq1$.

source.place: Matrix.det_isEmpty:94; constants: ContDiff/Basic.lean:111; agent zero-dimensional case

proof.text: Put $W_{ij}=x_i(U_i\cap U_j)$ and $F_{ij}=x_j\circ x_i^{-1}:W_{ij}\to W_{ji}$. These domains are open because the chart maps are homeomorphisms on open sets. Both $F_{ij}$ and its inverse $F_{ji}$ are smooth: for atlas charts this is the definition, and for charts compatible with the atlas, near any $u=x_i(p)$ choose an atlas chart $y$ at $p$ and write $F_{ij}=(x_j\circ y^{-1})\circ(y\circ x_i^{-1})$ on an open neighbourhood of $u$, a composite of smooth maps. The smooth differentiation lemma therefore gives differentiability and smoothness of $u\mapsto DF_{ij}(u)$ on $W_{ij}$.

source.place: ContDiffAt.fderiv_right:724; agent restriction to open chart overlaps

proof.text: For $u=x_i(p)$ put $v=F_{ij}(u)=x_j(p)$. The equalities $F_{ji}\circ F_{ij}=\mathrm{id}$ near $u$ and $F_{ij}\circ F_{ji}=\mathrm{id}$ near $v$, differentiated by the chain rule, give $DF_{ji}(v)DF_{ij}(u)=I$ and $DF_{ij}(u)DF_{ji}(v)=I$. Represent these maps by their standard real $m\times m$ matrices. Determinant multiplicativity gives $\det DF_{ji}(v)\det DF_{ij}(u)=1$; here $\det I=1$ follows directly from the Leibniz formula, whose only nonzero summand is the identity permutation. Neither determinant is zero, so $g_{ij}(p)>0$. Taking absolute values gives $g_{ji}(p)g_{ij}(p)=1$. Also $F_{ii}=\mathrm{id}$ and its derivative is $I$, so $g_{ii}=1$.

source.place: Matrix.det_mul:138; FDeriv/Comp.lean HasFDerivAt.comp:105; agent inverse-chart and identity calculations

proof.text: Write $d_{ij}(u)=\det DF_{ij}(u)$. Each matrix entry of $DF_{ij}$ is smooth: evaluation on a fixed standard basis vector followed by a coordinate projection is a continuous real-linear functional on the finite-dimensional space of linear maps. Expand the determinant by its finite Leibniz sum. Smoothness of sums, products and constants proves that $d_{ij}$ is smooth. At $u_0$ it is nonzero by step 3; continuity supplies a neighbourhood on which $|d_{ij}(u)-d_{ij}(u_0)|<|d_{ij}(u_0)|/2$. On this neighbourhood its sign is constant, and $|d_{ij}|$ is either $d_{ij}$ or $-d_{ij}$. Both are smooth by the scalar calculus lemma. Thus $g_{ij}$ is smooth in the $x_i$ coordinates. In any other compatible chart $x_t$, its expression is $|d_{ij}|\circ(x_i\circ x_t^{-1})$ on the appropriate open overlap, smooth by composition. This is precisely smoothness on $U_i\cap U_j$.

source.place: ContDiffAt.comp:223; ContDiff/Operations.lean add:184 and mul:450; agent finite determinant expansion and local sign argument

proof.text: Apply step 4 to the reversed pair of charts to obtain smoothness of $g_{ji}$. Since step 3 gives $g_{ji}(p)g_{ij}(p)=1$ with $g_{ij}(p)>0$, pointwise real division identifies $g_{ij}^{-1}=g_{ji}$. The reciprocal is therefore smooth. This uses no theorem about smooth inversion.

source.place: agent substitution of the reverse-pair identity from steps 3 and 4

proof.text: At a triple-overlap point put $u=x_i(p)$ and $v=x_j(p)$. On the open triple-overlap coordinate domain, cancellation of $x_j^{-1}x_j$ gives $F_{ik}=F_{jk}\circ F_{ij}$. The chain rule gives $DF_{ik}(u)=DF_{jk}(v)DF_{ij}(u)$. Determinant multiplicativity and the elementary real identity $|ab|=|a||b|$ give $g_{ik}(p)=g_{jk}(p)g_{ij}(p)$. All operations above occur on open Euclidean neighbourhoods of the point, so no orientation, Hausdorffness, countability or compactness assumption has been used.
